questions.q: Why is a random train/test split invalid for financial time series like the data behind SR-5?
options: Random splits only fail when the dataset has fewer than 1,000 rows
There is no issue with random splits for time series data
A random split can let the model train on data from after the test period, leaking future information it could never have had in real deployment
Random splits are always invalid for every type of data
questions.explain: A random split ignores time order, letting the model see future data during training — exactly what purged walk-forward validation (Lesson 8) was designed to prevent.

questions.q: What did the simulation of two completely independent random walks demonstrate about spurious correlation?
options: The simulation showed random walks are identical to white noise in every statistical property
Correlation between random walks is always exactly zero
Independent random walks never show meaningful correlation
Two unrelated random walks showed a mean absolute correlation of about 0.43, exceeding |r| = 0.5 in roughly 43% of trials, purely by chance
questions.explain: The verified simulation showed meaningfully high correlation (mean |r| ≈ 0.43, with 43% of trials exceeding 0.5) between two series with no real relationship at all — a concrete demonstration of spurious correlation risk.

questions.q: Why did SR-5 use Ridge regression rather than Lasso, given a feature set that is correlated across sectors?
options: Ridge regression requires no regularization parameter at all
Ridge is always faster to compute than Lasso regardless of the data
Ridge's L2 penalty shrinks correlated coefficients together rather than arbitrarily zeroing out some of them the way Lasso's L1 penalty tends to
Lasso cannot be used with any financial data
questions.explain: Given correlated sector-level features, Ridge's L2 penalty distributes shrinkage across correlated predictors instead of arbitrarily selecting one and zeroing the rest, which is the trade-off Lasso's L1 penalty makes.

questions.q: Why is Sharpe ratio preferred over R² or classification accuracy as an evaluation metric for a trading signal?
options: R² and accuracy are impossible to compute for trading strategies
There is no meaningful difference between these metrics for this purpose
Sharpe ratio is easier to calculate than R²
R² and accuracy measure fit to the data, not economic value, and can look fine while a strategy loses money after costs; Sharpe directly measures risk-adjusted return
questions.explain: The evaluation metric should reflect the real-world objective — risk-adjusted return — rather than a statistical fit measure that can look good while the strategy itself is unprofitable net of costs.

questions.q: What is a sound way to detect whether a strategy's edge has decayed over time, rather than relying on one aggregate backtest number?
options: Ignore recent performance and trust the original backtest indefinitely
Recompute the single full-sample Sharpe ratio repeatedly
Track rolling out-of-sample performance in fixed windows (e.g., quarterly) and compare against pre-specified kill criteria
Switch to a completely different strategy as soon as any single day is negative
questions.explain: Rolling, non-overlapping out-of-sample windows reveal whether performance is trending down over time, which a single aggregate Sharpe across the whole sample can mask.
